message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Policy Brief: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics
Riverside County Education Authority, Policy Unit, January 2026

Summary
In 2024-25 the Authority funded a pilot of high-dose mathematics tutoring for Year 7 pupils in six urban secondary schools. Pupils who received tutoring made substantially more progress than a randomly selected comparison group. This brief recommends extending the programme to all 42 secondary schools in the county from September 2026, at an estimated annual cost of £2.9 million.

The pilot
Tutoring was delivered in groups of three pupils, three one-hour sessions a week, for 30 weeks, during the school day. Tutors were undergraduate and postgraduate students from Riverside University, recruited, trained and paid £16 an hour through the University's Education Department. Pupils were eligible if they had scored below the expected standard in the end-of-primary mathematics assessment.

Of 480 eligible pupils in the six schools, 360 were offered places by lottery, because tutor capacity was limited; the remaining 120 formed the comparison group. Because places were allocated at random, the comparison is a fair one: the two groups had near-identical prior attainment, attendance and demographic profiles at the start of the year.

Results
Progress was measured using the standardised Year 7 mathematics assessment, taken in September 2024 and again in June 2025.

Group | Pupils assessed in June | Mean score, Sept 2024 | Mean score, June 2025 | Gain
Tutored | 342 | 88.0 | 98.6 | 10.6
Comparison | 114 | 87.8 | 93.4 | 5.6

Tutored pupils gained 10.6 points against 5.6 for the comparison group, a gain 89% larger. The difference of five points is equivalent to roughly four months of additional progress, and is in line with the effects reported in the national evidence base for small-group tutoring. Attendance at sessions averaged 87%, and 95% of the pupils offered a place completed the programme.

Teachers in all six schools reported that tutored pupils were more confident in lessons, and four of the six head teachers have asked for the programme to continue.

Proposal
We propose to extend the programme to all eligible Year 7 pupils in the county's 42 secondary schools from September 2026, retaining the design that proved effective: the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks, delivered in school hours by trained university-student tutors. Riverside University has agreed in principle to expand its recruitment, and its Education Department will continue to train and pay tutors.

Around 3,100 pupils a year meet the eligibility criterion across the 42 schools. Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus; the remaining 16 are in or near Riverside itself, within a short bus ride of the campus, as were all six pilot schools.

Cost
The pilot cost £750 per tutored pupil: £480 in tutor pay (90 hours of tutoring per group, shared among three pupils, at £16 an hour), £220 for university coordination and training, and £50 for materials and assessment. Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million.

This compares favourably with the Authority's current spending on Year 8 and Year 9 catch-up classes, which cost £1,100 per pupil and have shown no measurable effect on attainment in the last two internal evaluations. We propose that the catch-up budget be wound down over two years and the savings redirected to tutoring.

Risks and mitigations
Tutor quality. All tutors will complete the University's 12-hour training course and be observed twice per term by a school mathematics lead.
Timetabling. Sessions will be scheduled during form time and one weekly mathematics lesson, as in the pilot, so pupils do not miss other subjects.
Evaluation. The Policy Unit will continue to track progress using the standardised assessment and will report to Committee annually.

Recommendation
The pilot provides rigorous, randomised evidence that high-dose tutoring substantially accelerates progress for pupils who start secondary school behind in mathematics. The model is proven and its costs are known. We recommend that the Committee approve £2.9 million a year from September 2026 to extend tutoring to all 42 secondary schools, funded in part by winding down the catch-up class budget.
</document>
response:
# Review: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics

The pilot evidence is reasonably strong, but the proposal does not follow from it. There are two factual errors in the brief and one serious gap in generalisability.

## Errors that need fixing before this goes to Committee

**1. The headline cost doesn't match its own arithmetic.**
£750 × 3,100 pupils = **£2.325m**, not £2.9m. £2.9m implies about £935 per pupil. Either the unit cost, the pupil count or the total is wrong, or an uncosted adjustment (e.g. rural travel) was folded in without saying so. The Committee is being asked to approve a specific figure, so this must be reconciled.

**2. The proposal changes the delivery model while claiming to keep it.**
The pilot used groups of three. The Proposal says it will retain "the one-to-one format used in the pilot." If it really is one-to-one, tutor pay triples to £1,440 per pupil and the total cost is roughly £5.3m. If it is a typo, it should be corrected, because it undermines the claim that the "design that proved effective" is being kept.

## The main substantive weakness: the pilot doesn't cover most of the proposed schools

All six pilot schools were urban and a short bus ride from the university. 26 of the 42 proposed schools (62%) are rural and 40–75 miles away. The model depends on university students as tutors, so this is a major problem:

- **Tutor supply.** The pilot needed about 120 groups (about 360 tutor-hours a week). Full rollout needs about 1,030 groups, or roughly 3,100 tutor-hours a week, about 8–9 times the pilot. The brief only says the University "agreed in principle."
- **Travel costs and time.** Students cannot realistically commute 75 miles for a one-hour session. None of this is costed, and it likely explains part of any gap between £2.3m and £2.9m.
- **Fallback.** Remote or locally recruited tutors would be a different model with no evidence behind it.

The conclusion that "the model is proven and its costs are known" is therefore not supported for the majority of schools. A phased rollout, with urban schools first and a tested rural delivery model alongside, would fit the evidence better.

## Other issues

- **Costs omitted.** The brief doesn't cost school-side effort (twice-termly observations by maths leads in 42 schools), tutor recruitment at 8–9× scale, or the 12-hour training course for a much larger cohort. £220 per pupil for coordination may not hold at scale.
- **Overstated certainty.** "Rigorous," "proven" and "substantially" are strong for a single-year pilot in six schools. No confidence intervals, effect sizes or significance tests are reported, and there is no follow-up to show the gains persist. The "four months of additional progress" and "in line with national evidence" claims are asserted without sources.
- **Analysis basis.** Results use pupils assessed in June (342 of 360 and 114 of 120), not all randomised pupils. Attrition is similar in both groups (about 5%), which is reassuring, but the brief should say whether an intention-to-treat analysis was done. The "near-identical" baseline claim for attendance and demographics is not shown. Only the maths means are.
- **Weak supporting evidence.** Teacher reports and head teacher requests are anecdotal and shouldn't be presented alongside the trial results as corroboration.
- **The catch-up comparison.** The £1,100 per pupil catch-up classes are for Years 8–9, a different population, so this is not a like-for-like comparison. The wind-down takes two years while tutoring starts at full cost immediately, leaving a funding gap that the brief doesn't quantify. The "no measurable effect" finding comes from internal evaluations whose methods aren't described.
- **Timetabling.** Using one weekly maths lesson for tutoring means pupils miss part of their regular maths teaching. The brief says they don't miss "other subjects," which glosses over this.
- **Evaluation plan.** Tracking progress "using the standardised assessment" with no comparison group can't show whether the scaled programme works. If the rollout can't be randomised, a staggered start across schools would allow a fair comparison, especially for the rural schools where the model is untested.
- **Timing.** The brief is dated January 2026 and proposes a September 2026 start. If it is still going to Committee now, the start date needs updating.

## Suggested changes

1. Recompute the cost and state clearly what it includes (group size, rural travel, scale-up overheads).
2. Fix the "one-to-one" wording.
3. Add a section on rural delivery covering tutor supply, travel and cost, or limit the first phase to the 16 urban schools.
4. Tone down "proven" and add effect sizes with confidence intervals.
5. Show the catch-up savings timeline against tutoring spend year by year.
6. Build a proper evaluation into the rollout.

I can draft a corrected cost table or a phased-rollout option if you'd like.
